theme: Social comparison, through Epictetus' Enchiridion 1 (what is within our power and what is not)
hypothesis: A short spoken question hook that starts at once (voice from 0.1 s, a person with a phone in the first shot) keeps more viewers past 2 s than v008's statement hook after 0.5 s of silence.
hooks_considered: Everyone online looks ahead of you.
A Stoic's answer to comparing yourself to others.

philosophy.text: There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power.
philosophy.translation: Thomas Wentworth Higginson, The Works of Epictetus (Thomas Nelson and Sons, 1890; first published 1865), public domain

philosophy.text: Other people's results, and what anyone thinks of them, sit beyond your power.
philosophy.work: Enchiridion 1.1 lists reputation, property and office among the things beyond our power; 'results' is our modern reading

philosophy.text: Put your energy where your power is: your next step and how you spend today.
philosophy.work: Our reading of Enchiridion 1 (opinion, aim, desire and aversion are within our power)

sources.claim: Psychologists call this social comparison: without a clear measure, people evaluate their opinions and abilities by comparing themselves with others.
sources.title: Festinger, L. (1954). A Theory of Social Comparison Processes. Human Relations, 7(2), 117-140. doi:10.1177/001872675400700202

lines.text: It's late, you're scrolling, and everyone seems a little further ahead.
A new job, a new city, someone your age already doing the thing you keep planning.
Psychologists call this social comparison. When there's no clear measure, we size ourselves up against the people around us.
And online, you mostly see everyone's best days.
Almost two thousand years ago, the Stoic teacher Epictetus put it simply.
“There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power.”
Other people's results, and what anyone thinks of them, sit beyond your power.
You can still be happy for them, and still want things for yourself.
Epictetus only asks you to put your energy where your power is.
Your next step, and the way you spend today.
So tonight, put the phone face down.
Write one thing you'll do tomorrow that's fully yours. Small is fine.
A page, a walk, an hour of practice.
Their story was never your scoreboard.
You're on your own road, and the next step on it is yours.

post.caption: Comparing yourself to others gets loudest late at night. “There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power.” Epictetus, Enchiridion 1. What's one thing that's fully yours tomorrow? 🌙
